units: the metalworker describes his place of work as a living body
he gives the device that pushes air the role of a lung
he explains that without that air the burning weakens
he likens the block he strikes on to a shoulder
he presents the gripping tools as fearless fingers
he says those tools seize the glowing metal without flinching
he compares the hearth itself to an organ that beats
his student asks him which part she stands for in that body
he answers that she will be the memory of the gestures
text: The blacksmith spoke about his workshop as though it were a sleeping animal, and he would name its limbs one by one. The bellows, he said, stood in for the lungs: let that patient breathing stop, and the coals sank down, the bar of iron went cold. The anvil played the shoulder, since it received the whole violence of the hammer without a single flinch. The tongs, he added with a laugh, were fingers a great deal braver than his own, for they closed on glowing metal and never once trembled. As for the hearth, he called it a heart beating dully at the back of the room. His apprentice listened and never cut in, and afterwards she would ask which part of that body she stood for. She would be the memory, he answered, the one who kept the gestures once the old man's hands had given up.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: weaving started out as an entirely handmade operation
the earliest devices held the threads taut upright
lumps of clay served to keep those threads under tension
the worker put the crosswise thread in row by row
a treadle device then parted the threads to open a gap
the tool carrying the crosswise thread crossed the width in one move
a cord and a mallet then threw that tool mechanically
the pace doubled without calling for a second worker
punched cards later governed the lifting of each thread
the pattern moved from human memory onto a coded support
text: Weaving began in the fingers and only later ended up in machinery. The earliest frames held the threads upright, weighted at the foot with lumps of baked clay, and the worker pushed the crosswise thread through by hand, one row after another. Then came the treadle: press it down, and a whole group of threads lifted together to open a clean gap, so the shuttle could cross the entire width in a single throw. Someone soon tied that shuttle to a cord and a mallet, which flung it across on its own and doubled the pace without calling for a second worker. Later still, punched cards took over the lifting of each separate thread, and the pattern moved out of a weaver's memory onto a coded strip. Every stage took away a movement of the hand. Not one of them took away the eye that watches the tension.

units: the glassy layer is not paint laid on the surface
heat turns a mineral deposit into glass
the maker spreads a mix of powders on before firing
those powders melt and then spread into one continuous layer
cooling sets the material with no crystal structure
that lack of crystals explains the clearness obtained
sealing the pores keeps the liquid from seeping out
the hardness of the layer guards the wall against scratches
uneven shrinking between the two materials brings on a web of fine cracks
text: A glaze is not a coat of paint brushed onto a pot. It is glass, and the heat of the kiln makes it right on the skin of the clay itself. The potter covers the piece in a slurry of finely ground minerals and then hands it over to the fire. Under that heat the powders melt and spread into one unbroken layer; as they cool they stiffen again without going back to any crystal order, and that is where their clearness comes from. Because the layer seals the pores of the wall, water stops working its way through, so the vessel will hold a liquid. Because the layer is hard, it also guards the surface against scratches. Trouble starts, though, when the two materials shrink by different amounts: if the glass draws in tighter than the clay beneath, it splits into a web of hairline cracks.

units: a storage cabinet reaches the workshop out of true
its doors no longer shut properly
the joiner fears that taking it apart will break the old joints
wetting the panel fails because the curve returns on drying
planing the rebate makes the door gape on the far side
the maker notices that the twist does not run the whole height
he finds that a cracked rail is swinging the side panel
he puts a new rail in place of the split piece
he holds the frame under pressure until the glue sets
the cabinet stands plumb again and its doors work
text: The cupboard came into the workshop barely standing: one of its side panels had twisted badly out of true and the doors would no longer shut. Taking the whole thing apart was tempting, but the ancient joints would likely burst under the strain, so the joiner left them alone. He tried wetting the panel to draw it straight, and the wood curled back to its bend the moment it dried. He planed the rebate instead, and the door promptly gaped along the opposite edge. What solved it in the end was patient looking, nothing more. The panel was not bowed over its whole height; it swung around a single cracked rail. He cut a fresh rail, fitted it in place of the split one, clamped the frame until the glue had set hard, and hung the hinges again. The side stood plumb, and both doors swung true.

units: the text compares two ways of finishing the edge of a cloth
the hand method means folding the edge over twice
the iron serves to set each fold before the sewing
the hand stitches catch only one thread on the visible side
the hand finish calls for patience and moves along slowly
sewing done by hand ends up invisible on the right side
the machine method uses the same double fold
close pins hold the cloth before it goes under the needle
the machine finish stands up better to repeated washing
the machine stitching leaves a visible line on the outer face
text: Want a hem that hangs perfectly straight, with no ripples and no lumps? Look at both ways of doing it before you sew a single stitch. By hand, you fold the raw edge over, set the crease with the iron, fold it over a second time, and work blind stitches that pick up barely one thread on the right side. It takes patience and it will not be hurried, but the sewing disappears and the cloth keeps every bit of its drape. On the machine, you build the same double fold, pin it close all the way along, and then run it under the needle at a steady speed. It comes out tough, and it survives wash after wash far better than hand work does; in return, a line of stitching shows on the outside. So ask yourself what matters more to you: a hem that lasts for years, or a hem nobody ever notices.

units: a nonprofit teaches the metal trades to adults changing careers
the classes are held under the roof frame of an old market hall
the workshops are grouped by family of gestures
the first workshop teaches laying an even bead without burning through the sheet
the second deals with joining by pieces set in cold
the third takes up the finish obtained by heating and oiling
the last workshop teaches costing a job and buying stock
the woman in charge states that people rarely quit over technique
paperwork often wears the trainees down
text: Under the timber roof frame of an old market hall, a nonprofit teaches metalwork to adults changing careers, and its workshops are grouped by family of gestures. The first is given over to welding, where students learn to lay an even bead without burning through the sheet. The second covers mechanical joining, and every rivet there goes in cold, into a hole reamed carefully to size. The third handles the finish, and much of the talk turns on the patina you get by heating the piece and then oiling it. The last workshop is the surprise, since it deals with costing: pricing a job, buying the stock, promising a date you can actually keep. The woman who runs the place says that trainees rarely quit over technique. Paperwork is what wears them down. The next group starts at the close of the season.

units: the dye workshop smells of wet ash from first light
boards cover the vats while they are still cold
the water in the tubs keeps the color of the day before
the dyer lights a fire under the widest vat
she pulls a mass of undyed yarn out of a basket
steam climbs and the bath takes on the shade of crushed leaves
the wool that goes under takes up the color very fast
the next stage means rinsing the yarn in one tub after another
the yarn hung under the eaves drips and marks the ground
text: From first light onward the dye works smells of wet ash and of damp wool. The vats are still asleep beneath their heavy boards, and the water standing in them keeps the darkened color of the day before. Soon the dyer lights a fire under the widest of them all, then lifts a skein of undyed yarn out of a basket and shakes it out at arm's length to loosen the tangles. Steam climbs, the bath turns the shade of crushed leaves, and the wool goes under all at once, without a moment of hesitation, drinking up the color like a sponge. Rinsing follows: the skeins pass from one tub to the next, paler every time, and heavier between the fingers. By evening they hang in a tight row under the eaves, still streaming, and each one stains the ground below it with the shade that it has taken.

units: the writer disputes the idea that the electronic tool makes the old method useless
the optical device gives a vertical from its own footing
a settling of that footing throws the reading off with no visible warning
the hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts
the apprentice who handles that instrument grasps in his body what he is checking
younger crews no longer question what the screen shows
they do not confirm a reading by a second method
costly rework follows from this on site
the firm puts that rework down to carelessness
the writer holds that passing on the old skill is not nostalgia
text: To claim that an electronic instrument makes the plumb bob no longer worth learning is a failure of reasoning, and the cost of that error shows up on site. An optical device gives you a vertical at once, but it gives it from its own footing; let the tripod settle or the ground shake, and the error spreads with nothing at all to announce it. A hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts, and the apprentice who has held one grasps in his own body what he is checking. That understanding is missing now, and so the younger crews no longer think to doubt the screen, or to confirm a reading by some other means. Costly rework follows from it, which the firm puts down to carelessness when it comes instead of a training cut short. Passing on the older skill, then, is not nostalgia.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the instrument maker took over from her old master
the workshop was losing customers when she took it on
amateur players wanted an instrument that stayed in tune
those players could not pay for a piece shaped entirely by hand
she refused to work with a lesser wood
she split the making into two separate sets
the parts with no bearing on the sound come in batches from a workshop nearby
she shapes the pieces that settle the tone on her own
the price fell by a third with no loss of sound
her old master knew her hand on hearing the instrument
text: The instrument maker discussed here took over the workshop of her old master at the very moment when its customers were thinning out. She soon put her finger on a problem that no catalogue anywhere could solve: amateur players wanted an instrument that stayed in tune, and could not pay for one shaped from end to end by hand. Rather than come down to a lesser wood, she split her work into two distinct halves. The parts that have no bearing at all on the sound, the rough neck and the ribs, now come in batches from a workshop nearby. The parts that settle the tone, the belly and the bass bar, she cuts alone and trims by ear. The price fell by a third, the sound lost nothing, and her old master, who came by the shop to hear a finished order, knew her own hand in the varnish.

units: two runs of chairs are shown in the same room
the first run comes from a workshop attached to traditional joinery
that run uses fitted tenons and a back bent over steam
its sturdiness commands the reviewer's respect
its drawing looks unsure for want of attention paid to the outline
the second run comes from a studio using automated cutting
that second run is made in plywood
its seat meets the back with no cushion added
the object comes apart in a handful of moves
the reviewer holds that neither run clearly wins
text: Two runs of chairs share the same show room, and the pairing teaches you something. The first comes out of a workshop that stands by traditional joinery: tenons pared to fit, a back bent over steam, an oiled finish. Its sturdiness commands respect, and yet the drawing hesitates, as though the maker had spent all his care on the structure and left the outline to fend for itself. The second comes from a studio that makes no apology at all for plywood and automated cutting. The line is clean, the seat meets your back with no cushion added, and the whole thing comes apart in a handful of moves. The edges are dry, though, and no passing hand will ever soften them. Neither run clearly wins the day: one will outlast its owner, the other will charm the eye before it tires at the joints.
